title: Nitrone cycloaddition
subtitle: A nitrone and styrene give an isoxazolidine

reactants.caption: N-methyl-C-phenylnitrone + styrene
reactants.learnerPrompt: The nitrone is a 1,3-dipole. Its carbon and oxygen ends bond to the two alkene carbons in one step. Draw it.
hintTiers: The nitrone has C=N⁺–O⁻: three atoms, four π electrons. Add the alkene's two π electrons and six electrons move round a five-membered ring. Which end of styrene goes to oxygen?
The oxygen bonds to the alkene carbon carrying the phenyl group; the nitrone carbon bonds to the alkene CH₂. The C=N π pair goes onto nitrogen, which loses its positive charge. Three arrows.

Arrow 1: lone pair on the nitrone oxygen to a new bond to the phenyl-bearing alkene carbon. Arrow 2: from the alkene π bond to a new bond between the alkene CH₂ and the nitrone carbon. Arrow 3: from the C=N π bond to a lone pair on nitrogen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Valid cycloaddition arrows, but the other way round. With a monosubstituted alkene, the oxygen bonds to the carbon carrying the substituent, giving the 5-substituted isoxazolidine: the less crowded transition state, with the largest orbital coefficients matched.
Nitrogen is the middle atom of the dipole and makes no new bond. The ring closes through the nitrone carbon and oxygen.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: oxygen bonds to the phenyl-bearing carbon. Now the alkene CH₂ must bond to the nitrone carbon, which passes its C=N π pair to nitrogen. Two more arrows.

steps.explanationAfterStep: Another [3+2] cycloaddition: the nitrone's C–N–O unit and the alkene make a five-membered isoxazolidine ring, with no intermediate. The charges of the dipole cancel. The new ring carbons can carry their phenyl groups cis or trans; both form, and the app does not check stereochemistry yet.

mechanismSummary: Nitrones (R₂C=N⁺(R)–O⁻) are 1,3-dipoles that add to alkenes in a concerted [3+2] cycloaddition, giving isoxazolidines. With a monosubstituted alkene the oxygen bonds to the substituted carbon (the 5-substituted product). The N–O bond of the product is weak and can later be cut (e.g. with zinc and acid) to give a 1,3-amino alcohol, which makes this a useful synthetic method.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 34
